newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Lead firms battle over contract terms.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Lead firms battle over contract terms.

text.p: Traditional suppliers of lead to Southeast Asia are in a tough battle with Chinese and Taiwanese outfits to nail down supply contracts for 1997 and may have to trim their premiums to clinch some deals, traders said on Friday.

Australia's Pasminco and Canadian-based Cominco are fighting it out with Chinese and Taiwanese suppliers offering lead to Southeast Asian buyers at premiums ranging from US$60-$85 a tonne CIF, the traders said.

The two producers are seen offering premiums for long-term lead supply contracts next year way above these levels at between $120-$130 a tonne CIF, over London Metal Exchange (LME) cash prices, they added.
"Those two companies are knocking heads with this cheap material from China and Taiwan," a senior lead dealer with a Singapore-based commodity house said.
"We're seeing a lot of haggling over the supply contracts. The traditional companies are all in the same boat," he said.
Another dealer said both Cominco and Pasminco may have to reduce their premiums by about $10-$20 a tonne in order for them to clinch some deals.
"Those premiums will have to come down a bit," the trader said. "That's the only way for them to compete with the Chinese and the Taiwanese on this."
Dealers estimate negotiations on the long-term contracts for 1997 will run all the way to January before they are settled.

"There's no immediate rush for the buyers to book," one trader said. "What we've seen is a big push for Chinese lead. It's much more of a struggle for these two companies this year." Pasminco and Cominco offer reliable service and good quality lead, which is used primarily in the automobile battery industry around the region, traders said, and this will still allow them to maintain a significant premium over origins.
On the other hand, the lead being offered from China and Taiwan may be inferior in quality, but their huge discounts offer an attractive incentive to potential buyers, they said.
Lead's prospects going into 1997 appear to be promising as the car market in Southeast Asia is expected to grow vigorously on the back an increasingly affluent consumer base.
The rest of the base metal market in the region, however, has lapsed into a pre-Christmas holiday swoon, traders said.
"On a spot basis, the mood in the market is holiday-like. I don't think much will be done. People will just come back after the holidays," a dealer for a major Japanese trading house said.

Singapore-based dealers expect copper prices on the LME to trend slightly higher before the market slides into the doldrums next week when the Christmas and New Year holiday period goes into full swing.
"Most of the people are already on a holiday mode," another trader for a Japanese metal trading firm added.

LME copper stocks LME will probably post a small increase of about 2,000-3,000 tonnes while aluminium stocks are likely to slip by 500-1,000 tonnes when the LME report comes out later on Friday at 0900 GMT, traders said.
The amount of copper shipped to the LME warehouse in Singapore has slowed sharply, dealers said.
"I've not heard of any material that has come in lately," a dealer for a European metal trading firm said.
Prices of three-month copper were quoted by regional dealers at around $2,162/67 a tonne at 0330 GMT against London's late trade on Thursday of $2,162/65.
Three-month aluminium prices were seen at $1,554/58 a tonne at 0330 GMT compared with yesterday's late London trade of $1,552/54, the traders said.
Premiums in the city-state were also flat as demand slackened ahead of the holidays, traders said.
"It's going to be very slow," a dealer said.
